lead: A signal is measured by its size, its repetition and its symmetry. Energy and average power answer how large the signal is over all time. Periodicity answers whether it repeats. Even and odd symmetry answers whether it is a mirror image about zero. These labels decide which transform applies, whether a Fourier series exists, and which terms vanish. You meet them in a mains voltage waveform, a heart-rate trace, and a log of UPI transactions sampled every second.
prereq: You need signal notation and the continuous-time (CT) versus discrete-time (DT) distinction from Chapter 1.1.

sections.h3: Energy and average power measure size

blocks.text: Total energy adds the squared signal over all time. Average power divides energy by the length of the observation window, then lets the window grow without limit. A finite pulse has finite energy and zero average power. A never-ending finite-amplitude wave has infinite energy and finite nonzero average power.

blocks.where: E is total energy; x(t) is the CT signal; |x(t)|² is the normalised instantaneous power, the power x would deliver to a 1 Ω resistor; if x is in volts, E is then in joules.

blocks.text: P = lim (T → ∞) (1/T) ∫ |x(t)|² dt,  taken over −T/2 ≤ t ≤ T/2
blocks.where: P is the normalised average power (watts when x is a voltage across 1 Ω); T is the length of the averaging window in seconds; the window is centred on zero.

blocks.text: For DT signals replace the integral by a sum and the window length by the number of samples.

E = Σ |x[n]|²,  summed over all n
P = lim (N → ∞) (1/(2N + 1)) Σ |x[n]|²,  summed over −N ≤ n ≤ N
blocks.where: n is the integer sample index; 2N+1 is the number of samples from −N to N; E and P both have units of (sample value)², because 2N+1 is a pure count.

items: Energy signal: 0 < E < ∞ and P = 0. Example: a single rectangular pulse.
Power signal: 0 < P < ∞ and E = ∞. Example: a sine wave that never stops.
Neither: both E and P are infinite. Example: x(t) = t for all t.
Some syllabi call energy and power the size of a signal.

blocks.text: A periodic signal repeats after a fixed shift. The smallest positive shift is the fundamental period. A signal that never repeats is aperiodic.
x(t) = x(t + T) for all t
blocks.where: T is any positive period in seconds; the fundamental period T0 is the smallest positive T; the fundamental frequency is f0 = 1/T0 Hz and the angular frequency is ω0 = 2π/T0 rad/s.

blocks.text: In DT the shift must be an integer number of samples.
x[n] = x[n + N] for all integer n
blocks.where: N is a positive integer period in samples; N0 is the smallest positive integer period.

blocks.text: A DT sinusoid cos(Ωn + φ) is periodic only when Ω/(2π) is a rational number. If Ω/(2π) = m/N in lowest terms, then N0 = N samples. In CT, a sum of two periodic signals is periodic only when the ratio T₁/T₂ of their periods is a rational number; its period is then the least common multiple of T₁ and T₂. In DT, a sum of periodic sequences is always periodic, because two integer periods always have a common multiple.
An even signal is unchanged by time reversal. An odd signal changes sign under time reversal. The definitions use the same rule for CT and DT, with −t replaced by −n.

blocks.where: x(t) is the signal value at time t; −t is the reversed time; an odd signal must satisfy x(0) = 0.

blocks.text: Every signal splits into an even part and an odd part. Add and subtract the signal and its reversed copy.

blocks.where: xₑ is the even part; xₒ is the odd part; x(t) = xₑ(t) + xₒ(t) for every t.

items: cos(ωt) and a constant are even; sin(ωt) and t are odd.
even × even = even; odd × odd = even; even × odd = odd.
A signal with a nonzero average has a nonzero even part.

figure.caption: The sequence x[n] = 1, 2, 3 at n = 0, 1, 2 split into its even part (mirror image about n = 0) and its odd part (mirror image with a sign change). The two parts add back to x[n], and their energies 7.5 and 6.5 add to the energy 14.

examples.question: For x(t) = 6 cos(200πt) + 3 V, find the fundamental period T0, the average power P normalized to 1 Ω, the total energy E, and the even and odd parts.
steps: Compare with A cos(ωt) + DC. Here A = 6 V, ω = 200π rad/s, and DC = 3 V.
T0 = 2π/ω = 2π/(200π) = 0.01 s = 10 ms. The fundamental frequency is f0 = 1/T0 = 100 Hz.
Average power of A cos(ωt) is A²/2 = 6²/2 = 18 W. Average power of the DC term is 3² = 9 W. The cross term averages to zero over whole periods.
Energy over one period is P × T0 = 27 × 0.01 = 0.27 J. The signal repeats forever, so E = 0.27 + 0.27 + … = ∞.
cos(200πt) is even and the constant 3 is even, so x(−t) = x(t). Therefore xₑ(t) = x(t) and xₒ(t) = 0.
examples.check:
import math
A = 6
dc = 3
omega = 200 * math.pi
T0 = 2 * math.pi / omega
P = A**2 / 2 + dc**2
print(T0)
print(P)

examples.question: A DT signal is x[n] = 1, 2, 3 at n = 0, 1, 2 and 0 for every other n. (a) Find its energy E. (b) Find its even part xₑ[n] and odd part xₒ[n]. (c) Find the energy of each part and compare their sum with E.
steps: (a) E = Σ |x[n]|² = 1² + 2² + 3² = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. E is finite and the signal lasts three samples, so it is an energy signal with P = 0.
(b) Reverse the sequence: x[−n] = 3, 2, 1 at n = −2, −1, 0. Then xₑ[n] = (x[n] + x[−n])/2 and xₒ[n] = (x[n] − x[−n])/2, sample by sample, as in the table.
Check the symmetry: xₑ[−2] = xₑ[2] = 1.5, so xₑ is even; xₒ[−2] = −1.5 = −xₒ[2], so xₒ is odd, and xₒ[0] = 0 as every odd signal needs.

Eₑ + Eₒ = 7.5 + 6.5 = 14 = E. The energies add because the two parts never reinforce each other: Σ xₑ[n]xₒ[n] = (1.5)(−1.5) + (1)(−1) + (1)(0) + (1)(1) + (1.5)(1.5) = 0. Chapter 1.7 calls such signals orthogonal.

traps: A periodic finite-amplitude signal is a power signal, not an energy signal. Its energy is infinite, not zero.
Do not confuse zero average value with zero average power. sin(t) has zero mean but P = 1/2 for unit amplitude.
For DT sinusoids, periodic in n needs Ω/(2π) rational. A sampled sine can look periodic on paper but be aperiodic in the sample index.
In the even-part formula, divide by 2. Forgetting the 2 gives twice the even part.
An odd signal must pass through zero at the origin, so x(0) = 0. A signal with x(0) ≠ 0 cannot be purely odd.

quiz.q: Define an energy signal and a power signal in terms of E and P.
quiz.a: Energy signal: 0 < E < ∞ and P = 0. Power signal: 0 < P < ∞ and E = ∞.

quiz.q: State the condition for a CT signal to be even and the condition to be odd.
quiz.a: Even: x(−t) = x(t) for all t. Odd: x(−t) = −x(t) for all t.

quiz.q: Why does a periodic signal with finite amplitude have infinite energy but finite average power?
quiz.a: Each period adds the same positive energy P·T0. Infinitely many periods add infinitely many such amounts, so E = ∞. Dividing by the growing observation length T gives the finite average P.

quiz.q: Find T0 and P for x(t) = 4 cos(100πt) + 2 V, normalized to 1 Ω.
Find the even and odd parts of x(t) = 5 + 3t.
A DT signal is x[n] = cos(0.2πn). Is it periodic? If yes, give N0.
quiz.a: Ω = 0.2π, so Ω/(2π) = 0.1 = 1/10, a rational number. Yes, it is periodic with N0 = 10 samples.

quiz.q: Can a nonzero signal be both an energy signal and a power signal? Explain.
quiz.a: No. An energy signal has P = 0 and finite E. A power signal has E = ∞ and finite nonzero P. The two conditions are mutually exclusive.

beyond: Not for the exam. Energy and power labels carry into spectral density, where a power signal has a power spectral density and an energy signal has an energy spectral density; see Correlation and spectral density of signals. Even and odd symmetry shortens Fourier series work because cosine terms capture the even part and sine terms capture the odd part. In communications, average power sets battery life and heat in a transmitter. In biomedical instrumentation, energy of an ECG pulse helps detect abnormal beats. Search next for Parseval's theorem and power spectral density.
